Dan Kaminsky's discovery led to an emergency, coordinated patch across nearly every DNS vendor.
UDP has no handshake, so the source address isn't checked. Small question, huge answer, wrong destination.
Open resolvers are amplification weapons. A resolver should only serve its own users.
The random-looking labels are encoded data. The attacker's nameserver for x7k2.net reads it from the queries.
Signatures prove an answer is genuine and unchanged. They don't hide it.
DNSSEC doesn't encrypt anything. DNS over TLS or HTTPS hides the queries from the local network.
The DS (delegation signer) is a hash of the child's key, signed by the parent. Follow the DS records up and you reach the root.
Every signed set of records comes with an RRSIG.
DoT uses 853. DoH uses 443, so it looks like ordinary web traffic.
